script.opening: "I’ve come about Mia’s jabs, but honestly I’m not sure about the MMR. I’ve read quite a bit online — there’s stuff about it being linked to autism, and about overloading their little immune systems with so many vaccines. I’m not anti-vaccine or anything, I just want to do the right thing for her. What do you think?"

facts.text: Mia is 13 months, first child. Born at term, healthy, growing well, walking round the furniture, saying "mama" and "dada". Had all her baby jabs on time; had a fever after one of them and "was grizzly for a day".

No serious allergic reaction to any vaccine. No egg or gelatin allergy. Not on steroids or any medicines; no illness affecting her immune system. Nobody at home having cancer treatment. Mia is well today, no fever.
Facebook posts and a parenting forum; a friend shared a video about a boy who "changed after his MMR". Hasn’t read the NHS leaflet. "Then why do so many people still say it?"
Was told by the nursery nurse it is now "four in one" with chickenpox. Worried that’s even more for Mia’s body to cope with.

Lives with partner, Sam, who "thinks I’m overthinking it, he’d just get it done". Works part-time in a bank. Mia starts nursery 3 days a week next month. Lauren’s nephew (her sister’s son, 6) has autism — she has seen how hard it is for her sister.
Lauren thinks she had "all the usual jabs" as a child. Is planning another baby in the next year or two (only if asked about future plans).

Warm, thoughtful, anxious — not hostile. If lectured, given statistics without being asked about your worries, or made to feel stupid, become defensive and say you’ll "think about it" and leave. If the doctor asks what worries you most and listens, open up about your nephew. You may want a day or two to read something reliable before booking — accept an open door gratefully.

ice.ideas: "There might be a link with autism, and four vaccines at once might be too much for her."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of causing harm either way: "My sister’s little boy has autism. If I gave her the jab and something happened, I couldn’t forgive myself." She has not thought much about how serious measles can be.
ice.expectations: "Your honest opinion — what would you do?" Wants to be listened to, not pushed.

cues: "I’m not anti-vaccine or anything" — a hesitant, persuadable parent; explore, don’t lecture.
"I couldn’t forgive myself" — the fear of harm behind the questions.
"What do you think?" — an invitation for a clear, honest recommendation.

checkpoints.text: EXPLORES her specific concerns, sources and underlying fears, and elicits her understanding FIRST — using a non-judgemental, motivational-interviewing-style approach rather than lecturing

Addresses the AUTISM myth accurately (fraudulent original study, retracted by The Lancet in 2010; no link in subsequent large studies such as Hviid 2019) clearly and non-defensively, acknowledging why the fear persists
Addresses the "immune overload" myth and explains simply how vaccines/combined MMR work and are safe and effective

Balances the discussion with the REAL risks of the diseases (measles — pneumonia/encephalitis/death; mumps; rubella in pregnancy) and the importance of herd immunity/outbreaks — framing it as vaccine risk vs disease risk

RESPECTS her AUTONOMY — gives a clear recommendation and honest information without coercion/shaming, offers written info, time, a follow-up, and an open door if she declines today — checks for genuine contraindications, confirms consent is informed, voluntary and from a person with parental responsibility (Green Book chapter 2; GMC 2020), knows MMRV is now given at 12 and 18 months (UKHSA, from 1 January 2026), and documents the discussion
Reads her as an anxious, thoughtful parent (not an ideological refuser), builds trust, and engages her concerns warmly rather than dismissing or pressuring
Checks understanding, addresses each concern, and maintains a respectful, trust-preserving relationship throughout
Safety-nets and follows up: reliable information sources, a follow-up/catch-up plan, an open door, and clarity on the recommendation — informing and respecting autonomy, not coercing or lecturing

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you’re asking rather than just deciding — that’s a caring parent. Before I share what I think, tell me what you’ve read and what worries you most about it? I’d rather understand your specific concerns than just reel off facts."

"The autism link is the one that scares a lot of parents, so I understand it. Honestly: it came from a single study that was later found to be fraudulent and was withdrawn, and the doctor was struck off the medical register. Since then, studies of millions of children have found no link at all. The worry is understandable, but the evidence is really clear."

"On overloading — it feels logical, but a baby’s immune system deals with thousands of germs every day; the few in MMR are a tiny drop. Combining them into one jab is safe and means fewer needles for Mia, not more strain."

worked.lbl: The other side of the scales
worked.txt: "It’s worth weighing what we’re protecting against: measles isn’t a mild rash — it can cause serious chest and brain infections and, rarely, death, and rubella in pregnancy can harm a baby. As fewer children are vaccinated, we’re seeing outbreaks again. So it’s really small vaccine risk versus real disease risk."

"My honest recommendation is the vaccine — now called MMRV, as it also covers chickenpox, with a second dose at 18 months — but it’s your decision, and I won’t pressure you. If you’d like time, I can give you reliable information to read and we can talk again. The offer stays open — we can catch up the jab whenever you’re ready. And if you do go ahead, we’ll check first that there’s no medical reason to delay, such as a severe allergy or a problem with her immune system."
"Whatever you decide today, you’re welcome back to talk it through again — no judgement. Would written information and a follow-up chat help? I’ll note our conversation so we can pick it up easily."

f.learning: Vaccine hesitancy is best met by EXPLORING rather than lecturing: elicit the parent’s specific concerns, what they have read and where, their underlying fears (harming their child either way), and their current understanding first, using a respectful, motivational-interviewing-style approach — because a thoughtful, anxious parent who is lectured or shamed disengages, while one whose concerns are genuinely heard and addressed is far more likely to vaccinate. Address the AUTISM myth accurately and non-defensively: the original claim came from a study found to be FRAUDULENT and RETRACTED by The Lancet in 2010 (its author struck off the medical register), and subsequent large, robust studies of millions of children show NO link between MMR and autism (e.g. Hviid, Annals of Internal Medicine 2019) — acknowledging why the fear persists rather than dismissing the parent for raising it. Address the "immune overload" worry (a child’s immune system handles vast numbers of antigens daily; the few in vaccines are a tiny fraction, and combined MMR — now MMRV at 12 and 18 months under the UKHSA schedule from 1 January 2026 — is safe, effective and reduces injections) and explain simply how vaccination primes immunity. Balance the discussion with the REAL risks of the diseases — measles (pneumonia, encephalitis, deafness, death, rare SSPE), mumps (meningitis/orchitis), rubella in pregnancy (congenital defects) — and the importance of herd immunity and the outbreaks that follow falling uptake, framing the choice as small vaccine risk versus real disease risk. Crucially, RESPECT the parent’s AUTONOMY: give a clear, honest recommendation without coercion or shaming, and if she is not ready, offer reliable written information, time, a follow-up and an open door (vaccination can be caught up), documenting the discussion, checking for genuine contraindications (Green Book) and ensuring consent is informed, voluntary and given by a person with parental responsibility (Green Book chapter 2; GMC Decision making and consent 2020) — a trust-preserving encounter is more likely to lead to vaccination than pressure. The hidden agenda is an anxious, thoughtful parent seeking trustworthy guidance, not an ideological refuser; engage, inform warmly, respect autonomy and build trust.

knowledge.guideline: [1] UKHSA Green Book, chapter 21 (measles) · [2] UKHSA: changes to the routine childhood vaccination schedule from 1 July 2025 and 1 January 2026 · [3] The Lancet, retraction of Wakefield et al. (2010) · [4] Hviid A et al., Annals of Internal Medicine 2019 (MMR and autism, Danish cohort) · [5] GMC Decision making and consent (2020) · [6] UKHSA Green Book, chapter 2 (consent)
knowledge.summary: A hesitant parent is best helped by exploring her concerns first, then giving accurate, balanced information and a clear recommendation, respecting her decision and keeping the door open. Mia is now due MMRV, which adds chickenpox protection to MMR.

points.t: UKHSA [2]: from 1 January 2026, MMRV (measles, mumps, rubella and varicella) replaced MMR in the routine schedule. Children born on or after 1 January 2025 receive MMRV at 12 months and 18 months. For children born on or after 1 July 2024 the second dose moved from 3 years 4 months to the new 18-month appointment. At 13 months in 2026, Mia is due her first MMRV dose.

Ask what she has read, where, and what worries her most, before giving information. Reflect the underlying motive: she wants to protect her child. An approach that elicits and responds to concerns keeps trust; lecturing or shaming tends to entrench hesitancy.

The 1998 Lancet paper suggesting a link was fully retracted by The Lancet in 2010 [3], and its lead author was struck off the UK medical register the same year. Large studies since have found no link: a Danish cohort of over 650,000 children found no increased autism risk after MMR, including in children with an autistic sibling [4].

Children encounter vast numbers of antigens every day from food, skin and gut bacteria and common infections. Combined vaccines add a tiny fraction of this and mean fewer injections. Combining is not a strain on the immune system.

UKHSA Green Book [1]: measles can cause otitis media, pneumonia, encephalitis and death, and rarely subacute sclerosing panencephalitis years later; mumps can cause meningitis and orchitis; rubella in pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome. Measles is highly infectious, so falling uptake leads to outbreaks that also endanger infants too young to be vaccinated and immunosuppressed people.

Consent for a young child comes from a person with parental responsibility (Green Book chapter 2 [6]). GMC [5]: share information in a balanced way the person can understand, give your recommendation, and respect their decision. Consent must be voluntary: no pressure or coercion.

Record the discussion and her decision, offer reliable written information (NHS vaccination pages, UKHSA leaflets), arrange a follow-up conversation, and make clear that missed doses can be caught up at any time. Mention the new 18-month appointment.

Check for real contraindications per the Green Book [1] (for example severe immunosuppression or a previous severe allergic reaction to a component) rather than dismissing all concern; this also shows her questions are taken seriously.

Online articles and posts as the source; fear of harming her child either way explored.
Checked Mia’s health, immunosuppression and previous vaccine reactions (genuine contraindications).
Separated evidence-based concerns from misinformation; explained coincidental timing of autism signs.
Real disease risks named: measles complications, mumps, congenital rubella; outbreaks.

Idea (MMR may cause autism, immune overload), concern (being responsible for harm), expectation (trustworthy guidance).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan

She has not thought much about how serious measles can be — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.

model.text: Hello Mrs Hill, I’m Dr Morgan. Can you hear me okay? … Thanks for booking to talk this through. What would you like to discuss?

I’ve come about Mia’s jabs, but honestly I’m not sure about the MMR. I’ve read quite a bit online. There’s stuff about it being linked to autism, and about overloading their little immune systems with so many vaccines. I’m not anti-vaccine or anything, I just want to do the right thing for her. What do you think?

I’m really glad you’re asking rather than just deciding either way. You clearly care about getting this right for Mia. I will tell you what I think, but it would help me to understand your worries properly first. Is that okay?
model.why: Affirms her motive; asks permission to explore before informing

model.text: Yes, of course.
What have you read, and where did you come across it?
Just things online. Articles and posts people share.
That must be really unsettling to read when you’re the one deciding. Which worry sits heaviest with you: autism, or the number of vaccines?
The autism one. I couldn’t forgive myself.
I understand that. It sounds like you’re worried about harming her whichever way you choose. Is that fair?
model.why: Names the underlying fear of making the wrong choice

model.text: Yes. Exactly that.
Is Mia well at the moment? Any medical conditions, treatments that affect her immunity, or a serious reaction to a vaccine before?
No, she’s well. Nothing like that.
And what do you already know about measles and the other illnesses the jab protects against?
model.why: Elicits her understanding of disease risk

model.text: Not much, really.

Let me start with autism, since it matters most to you. The idea came from one small study in 1998. It was later found to be dishonest and was withdrawn by the journal, and the doctor behind it was struck off. Since then, studies of hundreds of thousands of children, including one in Denmark of over 650,000, found no link at all, even in children with an autistic brother or sister.
model.why: Accurate, non-defensive account of the autism evidence

model.text: Then why do so many people still say it?

That’s a fair question. Signs of autism often become noticeable in the second year, which is also when this jab is given, so the timing can look connected even though it isn’t. Parents who notice those signs after a jab are describing something real; the cause just isn’t the vaccine.
I hadn’t thought of that.

On overloading: every day Mia’s immune system meets huge numbers of germs from food, toys and other children. A vaccine adds a tiny amount. One more thing to mention: since January the jab at this age is called MMRV, which also protects against chickenpox. It’s still one injection.
model.why: Addresses overload; explains the current MMRV schedule

model.text: So it’s four in one now? Is that too much?
It’s the same idea: a tiny amount for her immune system, and protection from chickenpox as well. The second dose is now at 18 months.
model.why: Responds to the concern without dismissing it

model.text: About measles: it isn’t just a rash. It can cause ear and chest infections, and sometimes swelling of the brain, and it can kill. Mumps can cause meningitis, and rubella in pregnancy can harm an unborn baby. We’ve seen outbreaks in the UK as fewer children are vaccinated. So it’s a very small risk from the vaccine against a real risk from the disease.
model.why: Balances with real disease risks and outbreaks

model.text: I didn’t realise it could be that serious.
My honest recommendation is that Mia has the vaccine. But it’s your decision, and I won’t pressure you. What are you thinking now?
I feel better about it. But I’d like a day or two to read something reliable before I book.

That’s completely reasonable. I’ll send you the NHS and UKHSA information, and the nurse can book her in whenever you’re ready. If you have more questions, we can talk again. If you decide to wait, she can still have it later.

While she isn’t protected, if Mia has a high temperature with a spreading rash, or contact with someone who has measles, ring us before coming in, so we can protect other patients. Can I check what you’re taking away from today?
The autism study was false and big studies show no link. Her immune system copes easily. Measles can be serious. Read the leaflets and book when I’m ready.
That’s it exactly. I’ll note our conversation so whoever you see next knows where we got to. Thank you for asking these questions.
model.why: Documents the discussion; ends warmly with the door open

model.text: Thank you for not making me feel stupid.

social.t: Shared articles and social media are powerful sources. Ask what she has read and offer trusted alternatives rather than dismissing her sources.
Hesitant parents usually fear harming their child by action more than by inaction. Naming this helps.

legal.t: Green Book chapter 2: consent for a young child is given by a person with parental responsibility. It must be informed and voluntary; one person with parental responsibility can consent, but disagreement between parents needs care.
Childhood vaccination is not compulsory in the UK. Declining must not affect the family’s care or registration.

professional.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): give a clear recommendation while respecting the decision; record the discussion and any decision to decline.
The childhood schedule changed in July 2025 and January 2026 (MMRV, 18-month appointment). Out-of-date advice undermines trust.

community.t: High uptake protects babies too young to be vaccinated, pregnant women and immunosuppressed people; outbreaks follow when coverage falls.
NHS vaccination pages and UKHSA leaflets for parents on MMRV; health visitors can continue the conversation.

redFlags: Genuine contraindication: severe immunosuppression or previous severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component
Mia currently unwell with a high fever (postpone, not cancel)
Recent measles contact or fever with a spreading rash
psychosocial: Online articles and posts as the main source
Fear of causing harm either way
Wanting a trusted opinion without judgement
ice: Idea: MMR might cause autism; many vaccines might overload the immune system
Concern: being responsible for harming Mia
Expectation: an honest opinion from the doctor

playbook.diagnosis: “You’re a careful parent weighing up conflicting information. The evidence is clear that the vaccine doesn’t cause autism, and the diseases it prevents can be serious.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Mia’s immune system is like a huge library that adds new books every day from everything she touches and eats. A vaccine adds a few pages. It teaches her body what measles looks like before she ever meets it.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you just want to do the right thing for Mia and you couldn’t forgive yourself if the jab harmed her. Let me share what the evidence shows, and then it’s your decision.”
management.psychosocial: Affirm her care; offer trusted sources alongside what she has read online; follow-up conversation available with the GP or health visitor.
sharedPlan: Explore concerns first, then address autism and overload with accurate evidence
Explain the January 2026 schedule: MMRV at 12 and 18 months
Written NHS and UKHSA information; nurse appointment whenever she is ready
Document the discussion and decision; catch-up possible at any age
safetyNet: Ring before attending if Mia has fever with a spreading rash or measles contact
Door left open at every future contact

pitfalls.intro: The trap is winning the argument and losing the parent. Marks sit in exploring first, accurate information delivered warmly, and respecting her decision with the door open.

items.fail: Giving the evidence before finding out what she has read and fears.
items.why: Information that misses her actual concern doesn’t land.
items.fix: “Tell me what you’ve read and what worries you most.”

items.fail: Vague reassurance (“it’s perfectly safe”) without the evidence.
items.why: She needs a credible reason to trust you over what she has read.
items.fix: Retracted study, author struck off, large studies with no link.

items.fail: Talking about MMR at 3 years 4 months as the second dose.
items.why: The schedule changed: MMRV at 12 and 18 months for children born from 2025.

items.fail: Mocking what she has read online.
items.fix: “It’s understandable that worried you. Let me share what the large studies found.”

items.why: Pressure breaks trust and makes consent involuntary.
items.fix: “It’s your decision. Take the information home; book whenever you’re ready.”

items.why: A closed door lowers future uptake.
items.fix: Document, offer follow-up, remind her catch-up is possible.

Sources, the heaviest worry, fear of harm either way, Mia’s health and contraindications, her understanding of the diseases.
Autism evidence, timing coincidence, overload, MMRV and the 18-month dose, disease risks and outbreaks.
Clear recommendation; her decision; information and time; catch-up available.
Rash or exposure advice, teach-back, documentation, open door.

wordPics.fail: Launches into a lecture, dismisses online sources as nonsense, pressures her to book today, or accepts refusal without offering information; never checks what she knows about measles; states outdated schedule information.
wordPics.pass: Explores her concerns, explains the autism evidence and the overload myth accurately, describes the disease risks, gives a recommendation and respects her decision.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: names her fear of harm either way; explains why the timing of autism signs misleads; knows Mia is due MMRV under the January 2026 schedule; checks genuine contraindications; offers reliable reading, easy booking and catch-up; documents; she leaves feeling respected.

avoid.dont: “That study was nonsense and anyone who believes it is being silly.”
avoid.instead: “The worry is understandable. The study was later found to be dishonest and withdrawn, and large studies since show no link.”
avoid.why: Shaming entrenches hesitancy and loses trust.

avoid.dont: “If you don’t vaccinate, you’re putting other children at risk.”
avoid.instead: “Measles spreads very easily, so vaccinating also protects babies too young for the jab.”
avoid.why: Blame provokes defensiveness; the same fact framed as protection persuades.

avoid.dont: “We really need to do it today.”
avoid.instead: “It’s your decision. Take the information home, and the nurse can book her in whenever you’re ready.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A hesitant parent is best helped by exploring her concerns first, then giving accurate, balanced information and a clear recommendation, respecting her decision and keeping the door open. Mia is now due MMRV, which adds chickenpox protection to MMR.

points.t: UKHSA [2]: from 1 January 2026, MMRV (measles, mumps, rubella and varicella) replaced MMR in the routine schedule. Children born on or after 1 January 2025 receive MMRV at 12 months and 18 months. For children born on or after 1 July 2024 the second dose moved from 3 years 4 months to the new 18-month appointment. At 13 months in 2026, Mia is due her first MMRV dose.

Ask what she has read, where, and what worries her most, before giving information. Reflect the underlying motive: she wants to protect her child. An approach that elicits and responds to concerns keeps trust; lecturing or shaming tends to entrench hesitancy.

The 1998 Lancet paper suggesting a link was fully retracted by The Lancet in 2010 [3], and its lead author was struck off the UK medical register the same year. Large studies since have found no link: a Danish cohort of over 650,000 children found no increased autism risk after MMR, including in children with an autistic sibling [4].

Children encounter vast numbers of antigens every day from food, skin and gut bacteria and common infections. Combined vaccines add a tiny fraction of this and mean fewer injections. Combining is not a strain on the immune system.

UKHSA Green Book [1]: measles can cause otitis media, pneumonia, encephalitis and death, and rarely subacute sclerosing panencephalitis years later; mumps can cause meningitis and orchitis; rubella in pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome. Measles is highly infectious, so falling uptake leads to outbreaks that also endanger infants too young to be vaccinated and immunosuppressed people.

Consent for a young child comes from a person with parental responsibility (Green Book chapter 2 [6]). GMC [5]: share information in a balanced way the person can understand, give your recommendation, and respect their decision. Consent must be voluntary: no pressure or coercion.

Record the discussion and her decision, offer reliable written information (NHS vaccination pages, UKHSA leaflets), arrange a follow-up conversation, and make clear that missed doses can be caught up at any time. Mention the new 18-month appointment.

Check for real contraindications per the Green Book [1] (for example severe immunosuppression or a previous severe allergic reaction to a component) rather than dismissing all concern; this also shows her questions are taken seriously.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; welcomed the discussion; asked permission to explore before advising.
Online articles and posts as the source; fear of harming her child either way explored.
Picked up “I just want to do the right thing” and “what do you think?” and answered both.
Idea (MMR may cause autism, immune overload), concern (being responsible for harm), expectation (trustworthy guidance).
Checked Mia’s health, immunosuppression and previous vaccine reactions (genuine contraindications).
Separated evidence-based concerns from misinformation; explained coincidental timing of autism signs.
Real disease risks named: measles complications, mumps, congenital rubella; outbreaks.
Vaccine hesitancy in a caring parent; Mia due MMRV under the January 2026 schedule.
Clear recommendation, reliable written information, time to decide, easy booking, catch-up available.
Trust preserved; discussion documented; 18-month second dose mentioned.
Measles exposure and rash advice; follow-up conversation offered; door left open.

social.t: Shared articles and social media are powerful sources. Ask what she has read and offer trusted alternatives rather than dismissing her sources.
Hesitant parents usually fear harming their child by action more than by inaction. Naming this helps.

legal.t: Green Book chapter 2: consent for a young child is given by a person with parental responsibility. It must be informed and voluntary; one person with parental responsibility can consent, but disagreement between parents needs care.
Childhood vaccination is not compulsory in the UK. Declining must not affect the family’s care or registration.

professional.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): give a clear recommendation while respecting the decision; record the discussion and any decision to decline.
The childhood schedule changed in July 2025 and January 2026 (MMRV, 18-month appointment). Out-of-date advice undermines trust.

community.t: High uptake protects babies too young to be vaccinated, pregnant women and immunosuppressed people; outbreaks follow when coverage falls.
NHS vaccination pages and UKHSA leaflets for parents on MMRV; health visitors can continue the conversation.

redFlags: Genuine contraindication: severe immunosuppression or previous severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component
Mia currently unwell with a high fever (postpone, not cancel)
Recent measles contact or fever with a spreading rash
psychosocial: Online articles and posts as the main source
Fear of causing harm either way
Wanting a trusted opinion without judgement
ice: Idea: MMR might cause autism; many vaccines might overload the immune system
Concern: being responsible for harming Mia
Expectation: an honest opinion from the doctor

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “You’re a careful parent weighing up conflicting information. The evidence is clear that the vaccine doesn’t cause autism, and the diseases it prevents can be serious.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Mia’s immune system is like a huge library that adds new books every day from everything she touches and eats. A vaccine adds a few pages. It teaches her body what measles looks like before she ever meets it.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you just want to do the right thing for Mia and you couldn’t forgive yourself if the jab harmed her. Let me share what the evidence shows, and then it’s your decision.”
management.psychosocial: Affirm her care; offer trusted sources alongside what she has read online; follow-up conversation available with the GP or health visitor.
sharedPlan: Explore concerns first, then address autism and overload with accurate evidence
Explain the January 2026 schedule: MMRV at 12 and 18 months
Written NHS and UKHSA information; nurse appointment whenever she is ready
Document the discussion and decision; catch-up possible at any age
safetyNet: Ring before attending if Mia has fever with a spreading rash or measles contact
Door left open at every future contact

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is winning the argument and losing the parent. Marks sit in exploring first, accurate information delivered warmly, and respecting her decision with the door open.

items.fail: Giving the evidence before finding out what she has read and fears.
items.why: Information that misses her actual concern doesn’t land.
items.fix: “Tell me what you’ve read and what worries you most.”

items.fail: Vague reassurance (“it’s perfectly safe”) without the evidence.
items.why: She needs a credible reason to trust you over what she has read.
items.fix: Retracted study, author struck off, large studies with no link.

items.fail: Talking about MMR at 3 years 4 months as the second dose.
items.why: The schedule changed: MMRV at 12 and 18 months for children born from 2025.

items.fail: Mocking what she has read online.
items.fix: “It’s understandable that worried you. Let me share what the large studies found.”

items.why: Pressure breaks trust and makes consent involuntary.
items.fix: “It’s your decision. Take the information home; book whenever you’re ready.”

items.why: A closed door lowers future uptake.
items.fix: Document, offer follow-up, remind her catch-up is possible.
